The initiative is under the President Bola Tinubu Engineering Mentorship Programme.
The Minister of Works, Engr. Dave Umahi, announced the plan on Sunday while inspecting the ongoing construction of the Eleko Bridge at the endpoint of the Lagos section of the Coastal Highway.
The bridge features an innovative flyover with a U-turn on top.
Umahi said the project must benefit the young generation, noting that the mentorship programme directed by President Tinubu is very intensive but has not taken off.
“My immediate directive to the Controller of Lagos is that from Tuesday he has to set up his PRO to the engineering faculties, especially civil engineering departments of all the universities in Lagos State. We pay for it,” he said.
He tasked the Managing Director of Hi-Tech, Engineer Danny Abboud, to assign a technical person to take the students through every aspect of the project.
“Engineer Danny, we assign a technical person that will explain every aspect of this project from Chainage Zero to Chainage 103, which is the end of Sections One and Two. It is very important for them to learn what we are doing, and let them speak to what we are doing. Let them ask questions, and this will benefit our future,” he said.
Umahi described the Eleko Bridge as a masterpiece that is quite instructive, educative and innovative.
“This is quite instructive and educative and innovative. Engineer Danny, thank you. It can only be Hi-Tech that can do this,” he said.
He disclosed that the bridge has a clear span of about 50 metres, against the traditional span of 15 metres, while the clear span at the Dangote section is 70 metres to allow for the movement of heavy trucks at the refinery.
“We have clear span at the Dangote section, which we are going to, is 70 metres. That is to allow for fatal trucks movement at that refinery,” he said.
On the flyover, he said: “This flyover is quite innovative. You will join the service lane, and then if you are not keen on going forward on the coast highway, you can make a U-turn on top.”
“I’m very proud of Hi-Tech. I’m very proud of this legacy project. It is a beauty to behold, and I want us to show this at night. I think it’s out of this world,” he added.
Umahi expressed hope that the bridge will be completed by early January and commissioned separately because it is a masterpiece.
“We are very hopeful that this bridge will be completed early January, and it will be isolated commissioned because it’s a masterpiece,” he said.
The Minister said Section One, 47.47km by two, has been fully completed, while Section Two, about 53km by two, is also completed, apart from road architecture such as solar lights, underground drainage and walkway.
“It’s something that is out of this world in terms of performance, where you have over 200 kilometres plus being done within two years and half. It’s a performance that no other contractor in Africa has been able to achieve,” he said.
He described Hi-Tech Construction Company as performance-driven and integrity-driven, rather than profit-driven.
“If they are profit-driven, you would have seen variation upon variation because of the kind of terrain we are passing through. I want to thank the MD of Hi-Tech very highly and your management,” he said.
He said driving on the Coastal Highway is quite relieving, and challenged those threatening to stop the project.
“Some people will say, if I come as president, I’m going to stop the project. You, the people, should tell me whether you will like this project to be stopped,” he said.
Umahi said the same standard will be taken all the way from Lagos to Calabar, alongside other legacy projects including the 1,068km Sokoto-Badagry Highway, now over 30 per cent completed, and the 465km Trans-Sahara Highway, about 20 per cent done.
“When you ask, the money that is borrowed, what are they used for? They are being used for infrastructure. They are being used for investment in infrastructure,” he said.
He disclosed that many bidders are already asking to toll Section One and refund the money, but government is still putting finishing touches, including CCTV, rest houses and land for tourism and factories.
He added that the use of concrete pavement and solar lighting qualifies Nigeria for carbon credit claims, while windmill energy is planned along the coast to Calabar.
“It’s win-win for this country,” Umahi said, pleading with Nigerians, especially those from the eastern part of the country living in Lagos, to support the project.
“So we say to President Bola Tinubu that came at a very challenging moment, at a time that our country was at the verge of collapse, that your hands that have started this project selflessly, will finish this work by God’s special grace,” he said.
He urged Nigerians to appreciate what the President is doing, recalling as governor in 2023 how much a 50kg bag of rice cost and how much it costs now.
He argued that the economic indices of 2023 should be projected to now to ask where the country would have been.
He praised the President for eliminating scarcity of foreign exchange, noting that traders no longer need to go to the parallel market to buy dollars to import.
“But now, everybody has been leveled and corruption eliminated, so there is no scarcity of foreign exchange. There is no scarcity of dollar. The people can go to the central bank and they get dollar to do their importation. And there is also stability,” he said.
“What every investor in a country looks for is stability. And the president has brought stability from 2023 till now, and this is very important. Inflation is going down, and this is very very important. For once in three years, no ASUU strike. There are a lot to celebrate the president with,” he said.
He lamented that some people are keeping quiet whereas others are contracted on social media to darken counsel without knowledge, urging those who have savoured the air of freshness to speak out.
“When you see good things, you have to embrace it and you have to speak to it, so that good things will continue to be on your way,” he said.
Speaking on challenges on the road, Umahi said he has addressed the affront from local Okada drivers who wounded police and coastal guards, warning that it should not happen again.
He commended the security operatives for ensuring that stealing of metal fences and manhole covers is minimised, and for checking high speed on the road, Okada riders and broken-down vehicles.
